h1: AI Product Image Generator Tips From Your Phone
lead: Your shop's AI product photo generator can start with how you take the photo: your phone and window light. A plain gray running shoe can then sit on a white board, or in a room you name, without a studio day.
secondary_keywords: how to photograph products for an online store
summary: A true color and a readable shape are what you shoot for. Work at shoe height in window light, with filters off, then try a new setting from that same photo.

sections.h2: Give the Shoe a Fresh Setting
paras: The same gray running shoe can sit somewhere new, and it stays the shoe you ship. The phone photo on the white board is the start.
A bright outdoor table can make the shoe feel ready for sun or a trip. Check that the gray still matches the shoe in daylight.
A dry, open place gives the shoe a surface that feels rugged. Stone or a pale wall works. Watch the shadows so the edges stay clear.
A bare white board is the safest listing look, and a good start when you are unsure. A plain board or gray card is enough under the shoe.
A room you can name puts the shoe where a shopper already lives. A gym bench or a desk is enough. One sentence can say it: the gray running shoe on a white board in daylight.

sections.h2: How to Make Product Photos in 3 Simple Steps
paras: Upload the sharp phone photo of the gray running shoe, name the white board and the daylight, then download after you check the gray. That is the whole path from the phone to the file.
Upload Your Product Photo, or describe the picture in one plain line. Use the regular camera and keep the whole gray running shoe sharp.
Before that upload, rest the phone on books or a small tripod. Use the volume button or a short timer so the phone stays still when the shutter fires.
Fill most of the picture and leave a slim margin. Step closer instead of pinching to zoom.
Set the product beside a window in bright, indirect daylight, and turn the ceiling lights off. If sun hits the table, tape baking paper or a thin white sheet over the glass.
Warm bulbs mixed with daylight shift the color, and that shift shows up in later images too.
A plain board, gray card, or bare wood is enough behind the shoe. Wipe dust and smooth the laces before you shoot.
Hold the phone level with the shoe, and keep every edge inside the picture. The sole stays in frame when the phone is level with it.
Turn off portrait mode, filters, and beauty settings. They blur the background and change the edges and the color.
Tap the label to lock focus. If white areas lose all detail, lower the brightness until you can see the texture.
Take a straight side, then a three-quarter front and the sole while the setup is still out. Each of those needs its own photo of the shoe. Stay with the gray running shoe for every shot.
Upload each side of the shoe you care about, and only a side the photo actually showed. Zoom until the edges are clear, and compare the gray with the real shoe in daylight.
Upload the original file, not a screenshot or a picture that passed through a chat app. JPG, JPEG, PNG, WebP, BMP, TIF, and TIFF work. HEIC and HEIF work too. The limit is 32 MB.
Describe Your Scene. Name the shoe, the surface, and the light in one sentence. Save the price for your own editor. Decide the place before it runs, and say it the way you would say it to a friend.
Download and Post after you hold the real shoe beside the screen. Check the color, the edges, and the shape. Fix it with a follow-up sentence if needed. Add the price later in your own editor.
Open [lifestyle photos](page:lifestyle-photos), [change the background](page:change-background), or a [white background](page:white-background).
The same still of the shoe can start [AI image to video](page:image-to-video) when the listing also needs a short video.

faq.q: What does a product photo tool do for a shop?
faq.a: It puts the gray running shoe you photographed into a setting you name. A white board is one setting. The shoe in the file still has to match the shoe you ship.

faq.q: How does the shoe photo get made?
faq.a: Start with a photo where the whole running shoe is sharp. Say where it should sit, such as a white board. The picture comes back in that setting.

faq.q: What should I look for before I publish?
faq.a: The edges must be clear, the gray must match daylight on the real shoe, and no side should appear that your photo never showed.

faq.q: Can I use a product photo tool for free?
faq.a: No. One image is 24 credits. Plans are on [pricing](page:pricing): Starter is $24.50 a month for 200 credits, Pro is $35 for 300, and Premium is $63 for 600. The cost shows before the job starts.

faq.q: Are these photos useful on a product page?
faq.a: Yes. A product page can use the shoe photo, and an ad can use a second file of the same shoe with a different crop.

faq.q: Why use a new photo of the same shoe?
faq.a: You can see a new place around the shoe before you rent anything. If the place looks wrong, you still have the original phone photo.

faq.q: Can I sell with these photos?
faq.a: Yes. The download has no watermark, so the store page and a paid ad can both use the shoe photo. If a marketplace asks you to confirm you may use the file, your plan terms are the place to read.

faq.q: Do I need a camera, or is a phone enough?
faq.a: A phone is enough for the running shoe. Window light, filters off, and the whole shoe in the frame matter more than the camera body.
